## Abstract

Financial-inclusion policy in sub-Saharan Africa rests on the premise that credit moves smallholders toward best-practice technology. We ask whether it does in Ghana, using the 2012/13 and 2016/17 Ghana Living Standards Survey: `r fmt_num(objs$sample$n_pooled, 0)` crop farmers, `r fmt_pct(objs$treatment$share_treated, 1)` in borrowing households, with group-specific stochastic frontiers enveloped by a metafrontier and credit users matched one-to-one to non-users. Contrary to that premise, credit users' technology set lies `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points farther from the best-practice frontier than matched non-users'; technical efficiency within groups differs little and inconsistently in sign; and meta-frontier efficiency is `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points lower, almost entirely from that gap. They also apply fewer purchased inputs per hectare without producing less. The gap is robust to specification and pervasive across subgroups, cocoa excepted. These are associations, not causal effects. Most loans are informal and fewer than one in three financed farming: the question is less how much credit reaches farms than what it buys.

**Keywords**: financial inclusion; credit; mobile money; technical efficiency;
meta-stochastic frontier; Ghana

**JEL Classification**: G21, G51, O13, Q12, Q14
